Effect of microaerobic microbial pretreatment on anaerobic digestion of a 
lignocellulosic substrate under controlled pH conditions 
Haipeng Xu a,b, Yan Li b, Dongliang Hua b, Yuxiao Zhao b, Lei Chen b, Lei Zhou c, Guanyi Chen a,* 
a School of Environment Science and Engineering, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China 
b Energy Institute, Qilu University of Technology(Shandong Academy of Sciences), Shandong Key Laboratory of Biomass Gasification Technology, Jinan 250014, China 
c Shandong Pharmaceutical Industry Design Institute, Jinan 250100, China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• Proteiniphilum and Rummeliibacillus 
were 
dominant 
during 
mirobial 
pretreatment. 
• Pretreatment enhanced hydrolysis and 
acidogenesis of lignocellulose. 
• Both pH and pretreatment time greatly 
affected methane yield. 
• The highest methane yield was found at 
pH 8 and 12 h of pretreatment.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Lignocellulosic substrate 
Microaeration microbial pretreatment 
Hydrolysis 
Microbial community 
Methane 
A B S T R A C T   
The effects of various microaeration strategies and process parameters on anaerobic digestion (AD) of ligno­
cellulosic substrates have received increased attention; however, different results have been reported. To 
determine optimal conditions and clarify the mechanisms influencing this process, the effect of pretreatment of 
microaerobic microbial on corn stover decomposition and AD was investigated with real-time pH control. Fresh 
cow manure was chosen as the inoculum, as it has the strongest cellulose hydrolysis capacity under microaer­
ation conditions. Microaeration microbial pretreatment effectively promoted the hydrolysis and acidogenesis of 
corn stover, and pH considerably affected total solid reduction, volatile fatty acid (VFA), and accumulation of 
soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD) patterns by shifting microbial communities. Different pH levels and 
pretreatment times led to positive and negative effects on methane yield. A 12-h pretreatment of substrate at pH 
8 prior to AD increased the methane yield by 16.6% in comparison with the un-pretreated sample.   
1. Introduction 
China has strived to vigorously develop the anaerobic digestion (AD) 
of agricultural wastes to produce bio-natural gas since 2015 for 
environmental protection, renewable energy alternatives, and CO2 
emission reduction. Corn stover, accounting for about 32.5% of agri­
cultural straw produced in China, was regarded as a good candidate. 
Many biogas and bio-natural gas projects using corn stover as the main

substrate have been built and operated in China in recent years, but the 
project profit depends on government subsidies has limited rapid 
development. The low degradation efficiency due to the recalcitrant 
structure of lignocellulose is one of the important limiting factors 
(Woiciechowski et al., 2020). 
It is well known that pretreatment is an effective measure for 
improving digestion rate, thereby enhancing methane generation from 
lignocellulosic substrates. Many pretreatment technologies, such as 
alkaline, acid and steam explosion, are investigated for improving the 
lignocellulosic biomass AD (Frigon et al., 2012), with good results 
achieved. However, these pretreatment technologies usually have spe­
cific drawbacks, such as increased energy consumption, inhibitor for­
mation, or scaling-up difficulties. As a result, few of them have been 
used in commercial production, because of negative economic profit or 
the introduction of pollution. 
Accordingly, enhanced microbial hydrolysis pretreatment under 
microaeration conditions is considered an effective method to improve 
the AD of lignocellulosic substances by promoting certain facultative 
and aerobic microbial activities, while this increases biomass dissolution 
(Botheju & Bakke, 2011). However, the effect of microaeration on the 
AD of lignocellulose substances remains controversial. It is extensively 
reported that microaeration has positive effect (Fu et al., 2016; Lim & 
Wang, 2013), but some studies found that the addition of oxygen dete­
riorated AD, leading to reduced methane yield (Johansen & Bakke, 
2006). The uncertain outcomes may arise from different microaeration 
strategies, techniques, or intensities. 
As reported in previous studies, microaeration improves the methane 
potential of biomass by effectively promoting hydrolysis and acido­
genesis of complex substrates into simple organic matter (Nguyen et al., 
2019). Hydrolysis, which is positive for AD, and consumption of sub­
strate, which is negative for AD, exist in the pretreatment process. It can 
be speculated that if oxygen is supplied improperly, or if the pretreat­
ment time is too long, then oxygen respiration is too high and the 
availability of substrates for AD is decreased too much, leading to an 
adverse impact on AD. To maximize methane yield, pretreatment should 
be controlled to maximize the hydrolysis of lignocellulose while simul­
taneously minimizing chemical oxygen demand losses. 
There are two kinds of microaeration strategies used for enhancing 
the AD of biomass (Chen et al., 2020): one is to dose a little amount of 
oxygen (dissolved oxygen DO, 0.1–1.0 mg/L) or air to an anaerobic 
bioreactor (Nguyen & Khanal, 2018), and the other is to carry out the 
microaeration process as a pretreatment before AD in a separate reactor. 
The latter strategy has been adopted in many biogas projects using 
lignocellulosic substrates as feedstock. However, the effects of micro­
aerobic pretreatment and pretreatment process parameters on the AD 
performance of lignocellulosic substrates and the influencing mecha­
nisms of the process are less reported. The pH and length of pretreatment 
are important controllable parameters for pretreatment outcomes. The 
present work examined how pH and the length of microaerobic micro­
bial pretreatment (MMP) affected the corn stover AD. Besides, inoculum 
type, total solid (TS) loss, organic acid production, cellulase activity, and 
microbial community structure were also studied to reveal the mecha­
nism of positive and negative effects of MMP on the AD performance of 
corn stover. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Raw material and inoculum 
This study obtained the dry corn stover in the Licheng District, Jinan, 
China. Fresh cow manure, which contained 131.6 g/L TS, was collected 
from Jinan Jiabao Dairy Co., Ltd., and stored at 4 ◦C for no more than 7 
d before use. We obtained the anaerobic sludge containing 38.09 g/L 
volatile solids (VS) and 63.26 g/L TS in the mesophilic digestion tank of 
the upflow anaerobic sludge blanket in Shandong Xingguang Sugar 
Group Co., Ltd., Dezhou, China. 
2.2. Experimental methods 
2.2.1. MMP process 
Open reactors with water jackets and mechanical mixers were used 
to conduct the MMP. Corn stover and inoculum were mixed at a TS ratio 
of 3:1, followed by the addition of water until the TS content was 7.5%. 
The temperature in all reactors was maintained at 35 ◦C. Initially, the 
reactors were then subjected to 5 min of N2 flushing for achieving sol­
uble air replacement. Subsequently, the DO concentration was kept in 
the range of 0.1–1 mg/L. This concentration range was found to provide 
microaeration conditions for microaerophilic and facultative microbes 
(Wu et al., 2015). Such conditions may be achieved by mixing in open 
air. An online DO detector was used to monitor the DO concentration in 
the broth. The pH and pretreatment time were the examined variables at 
different levels in this study. The examined pH range of the pretreatment 
experiment was 5 to 8, which can be formed through process control or 
can take place spontaneously. The pH was controlled in real-time with a 
pH controller composed of a pH sensor, pH control unit, and charging 
pump; 1 M HCl or 1 M NaOH was added when the pH deviated from set 
limits. Each test was performed in triplicate. Pretreatment slurry sam­
ples collected for testing were stored at −20 ◦C before analysis. 
2.2.2. TS reduction test of corn stover during MMP 
We used a cutting mill to cut corn stover into small pieces, and then a 
10–20 mesh was used for filtering. To reduce the experimental error, the 
TS reduction of corn stover in the MMP was investigated by enclosing 
the substrates in nylon bags (pore size, <100 μm). (This step was an 
innovation of the current work). Then, approximately 1.0 g dry substrate 
was added to the nylon bag, the bag was then sealed thermally, and 
added to the MMP reactor. The substrate sealed in the bag was able to 
contact microaerobic microbes. Each nylon bag was obtained following 
pretreatment and rinsed by running water, following by drying within 
the oven under 105 ◦C. The TS of the substrate before and after pre­
treatment was weighed to calculate TS reduction. 
2.2.3. Experimental setup for AD 
The automatic methane potential test system (Bioprocess Control, 
Lund, Sweden) was used to determine the methane production of sub­
strates. This system can determine methane generation of diverse sam­
ples as time goes by. For diverse samples, their AD was conducted within 
the 500 mL bottles in batches. The anaerobic sludge was mixed with 
substrates at 3:1 (VS) into the bottles (Li et al., 2013). Thereafter, the 
resultant mixtures were subjected to incubation under 38 ◦C. Addi­
tionally, we selected another bottle that contained inoculum, without 
substrate to operate at the same conditions as control. Each blank and 
tests were conducted thrice. Finally, the endogenous control production 
was subtracted to obtain the net methane production. 
2.3. Analytical methods 
The approaches to examine wastewater and water were used to 
determine VS and TS (APHA, 2005). To determine soluble chemical 
oxygen demand (sCOD), we collected the sample supernatants obtained 
after 10 min of centrifugation at 12 000 rpm. sCOD was determined 
using a 5B-3B (V8) water quality detector (Beijing Lianhua Technology 
Co., Ltd., China). 
Then, the fiber analyzer (ANKOM 220, USA) was employed to 
determine lignin, hemicellulose, cellulose and the soluble substances in 
corn stover by Van Soest et al.’s method (1991). We also determined the 
amounts of neutral detergent fiber (NDF), acid detergent lignin (ADL) 
and acid detergent fiber (ADF) within dry samples. To be specific, sol­
uble substance levels were determined to be the difference of TS with 
NDF, while hemicellulose level was measured to be the difference of 
ADF with NDF, the cellulose level was measured to be the difference of 
ADF with ADL, whereas lignin equaled to ADL. 
The Agilent 7890 series gas chromatography system was adopted to

determine the concentrations of volatile fatty acids (VFAs; acetic, pro­
pionic, butyric, isobutyric, valeric, and isovaleric acids). Prior to VFA 
measuring, sample pretreatment was completed. After centrifugation, 
samples were subjected to acidification using the 3% phosphoric acid 
until the pH value was below 2, for the sake of converting fatty acids to 
the corresponding undissociated states. Thereafter, deionized water was 
used to dilute samples so that the VFA contents were within the standard 
curve range, meanwhile, the 0.22-μm filters were used for filtering. In 
this experiment, we used the HP-FFAP column (dimension, 50 m × 320 
μm × 0.5 μm). Additionally, we adopted the flame ionization detector, 
with the operating temperature being set at 300 ◦C. In addition, the 
nitrogen carrier gas was injected constantly at 30 mL/min, with an inlet 
temperature being 250 ◦C. The original temperature of the oven was 
60 ◦C, which was then heated at a 10 ◦C /min heating rate to 100 ◦C. The 
temperature at 100 ◦C was held for 2 min, then the temperature of the 
oven slowly elevated at 10 ◦C /min to 250 ◦C. 
2.4. Extracellular carboxymethyl cellulase assays 
The pretreatment slurry was subjected to 10 min of centrifugation at 
12 000 rpm and 4 ◦C to obtain the supernatants for enzyme assays. 
Ghose (1987) was adopted to assay the carboxymethyl cellulase 
(CMCase). Later, 1 mL of the 0.05 M pre-heated acetate buffer (pH 6.0) 
that contained carboxymethyl cellulose (0.5%, w/v) was added into the 
0.5 mL supernatants. Afterwards, the resultant mixture was subjected to 
1 h of incubation under 50 ◦C. Besides, Miller’s dinitrosalicylic acid 
approach Miller (1959) was utilized to assay the production of reducing 
sugars within the enzyme-exposed samples. Under the experimental 
conditions, one enzyme unit referred to the enzyme volume releasing 1 
mmol/min reducing sugars. 
2.5. Kinetic study 
The methane yield potential and the hydrolysis constant during AD 
was estimated using the first-order kinetic equation, which was written 
as: 
Bt = B0(1 −e−kt)
(1) 
where Bt stands for the accumulated methane amount generated at 
time t (d) (unit, L CH4/g TS), B0 represents the potential of methane 
production (L CH4/g TS), while k indicates the constant of hydrolysis 
kinetics (d−1). The Curve Expert (version 1.4) was used to adjust the 
paired experimental data (B, t) through non-linear regression, which 
made it possible to calculate k, R2 and B0 at 95% confidence interval (CI) 
for every case investigated. 
2.6. Microbiological analysis 
High-throughput sequencing was used to analyze the microbial 
community structure of pretreatment slurry before and after five days of 
MMP. We used the centrimonium bromide approach to extract the total 
genomic DNA. Later, we applied specific primers (including 16S V4: 
515F- 806R, 18S V4: 528F-706R, and 18S V9: 1380F-1510R) that had 
barcodes to amplify diverse regions in 16S rRNA/18SrRNA/ITS genes 
(16S V4/16S V3/16S V3-V4/16S V4-V5, Arc V4, ITS1/ITS2 and 18S V4/ 
18S V9). Each PCR procedure was conducted using the Phusion® High- 
Fidelity PCR Master Mix (15 µL, New England Biolabs, USA). Thereafter, 
the Qiagen Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen, Germany) was employed to pu­
rify PCR products. 
We adopted the TruSeq ® DNA PCR-Free Sample Preparation Kit 
(Illumina, USA) to generate sequencing libraries in accordance with 
specific protocols, followed by the addition of index codes. Besides, the 
Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system and the Qubit@ 2.0 Fluorometer 
(Thermo Scientific, USA) were employed to assess the quality of li­
braries. At last, the Illumina NovaSeq platform was adopted for 
sequencing the libraries, which produced the paired-end reads (250 bp 
in length). In addition, Uparse (Uparse v7.0.1001, http://drive5.com/ 
uparse/) was applied in sequence analysis (Edgar, 2013). At last, we 
deemed sequences that showed ≥97% similarity as the identical oper­
ational taxonomic units (OTUs). 
2.7. Calculation methods 
SPSS22.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, USA) was adopted for data analysis. 
All results were expressed as mean ± SD. Statistical significance was 
determined by analysis of variance (ANOVA). We deemed the signifi­
cance level as p < 0.05. In the presence of statistical significance, the 
means were separated using Tukey’s HSD test. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of inoculum type on MMP 
The MMP efficiency is mostly determined by certain facultative hy­
drolytic microbes that have the ability to degrade lignocellulose, it is 
important to have as many microbes as possible in the inoculum (Wen 
et al., 2015); the choice of inoculum for pretreatment is important. 
Composing microbial agent, cow manure, aerobic sludge, and anaerobic 
sludge were tested for their cellulose hydrolysis ability under MMP in 
this study. 
The filter paper weight loss method was adopted to record the cel­
lulose hydrolysis activity. Ashless filter paper packed in a nylon bag was 
added to the reactor during MMP with different inocula for 2 d. The dry 
weight of the paper was weighed before and after pretreatment. The 
results showed that the usage of composing microbial agent, aerobic 
sludge, and anaerobic sludge as inocula did not lead to significant TS 
reduction, whereas the fresh cow manure inoculation test led to prom­
inent filter paper TS loss (10.8%). Hence, it was concluded that the 
microbial community in fresh cow manure can effectively hydrolyze 
lignocellulose under microaeration conditions. Fresh cow manure was 
used as the inoculum in the next MMP experiment. The results of the 
aerobic and anaerobic sludge inocula are consistent with the reports of 
Yu et al. (2017) and Tsapekos et al. (2017). 
3.2. Hydrolysis and acidogenesis of corn stover at different pH MMP 
3.2.1. TS reduction of corn stover during MMP 
As reported in previous studies, hydrolysis accounts for a rate- 
limiting link during the organic matter AD process (Song et al., 2019), 
especially lignocellulosic material. In this study, all the microaeration 
pretreatment experiments maintained a DO concentration between 0.1 
and 1.0. g/L. This DO concentration may enhance solubilization of the 
organic matter by promoting the activity of microaerophilic and facul­
tative microorganisms (Botheju & Bakke, 2011). The TS reductions of 
corn stover, sCOD accumulation, total VFA concentration, NH4-N con­
centration, and extracellular CMCase activity were measured at 
different processing times (1 d, 2 d, 3 d, 4 d, 5 d) under different pH 
control strategies (pH 5, pH 6, pH 7, pH 8, and an uncontrolled pH (pH- 
U)) (Fig. 1). MMP effectively promoted hydrolysis of corn stover 
(Fig. 1a). Comparing different pH control strategies, it can be seen that 
TS reduction was greatly affected by pH during MMP. The hydrolysis 
sequence of the samples was pH 8 > pH 7 > pH-U > pH 6 > pH 5. This 
result is consistent with Zhang et al. (2012), and differs from that of 
Chen et al. (2007), whose experimental results showed that the hydro­
lysis of lignocellulose-type sludge at different pH values was in the 
following order: alkaline > acidic > neutral/blank test. After 5 d of 
pretreatment, the highest TS reduction reached 16.8% at pH 8, which 
was 33.9% higher than that of the pH-U sample. The lowest TS reduction 
reached 9.7% at pH 5, which was 30.6% lower than that of the pH-U 
sample. The slow rate of hydrolysis under acidic conditions may be 
due to the inhibition of microbial hydrolysis, as mentioned by Van 
H. Xu et al.

taking place at pH = 5 was associated with the pH value because of the 
impact on undissociated acid content.

diverse pH values to calculate changes in composition (Table 1). The 
results indicated that soluble components accounted for a large pro­
portion of TS reduction during pretreatment, especially on the first day. 
The proportion of lignin increased after MMP, because the degradation 
of cellulose and hemicellulose was faster than that of lignin. There was 
no obvious difference between the degradation rates of cellulose and 
hemicellulose, differing from Fu et al. (2015), who found that hemi­
cellulose and lignin were degraded faster than cellulose by 
microaeration-enhanced AD of corn straw. 
3.2.2. sCOD accumulation and organic acid production during MMP 
MMP elevates the sCOD content and promotes solubilization, which 
plays an important role in promoting methane generation. The sCOD of 
hydrolysate was greatly affected by pH (Fig. 1b). At pH 5, after an in­
crease in the first day, the sCOD concentration declined over time. The 
sCOD concentration at pH 6 began to decline slowly after 2 d, while at 
pH 7 and pH 8, the sCOD concentrations increased over time. 
After 5 d of pretreatment, the order of sCOD concentration in the 
hydrolysate was consistent with the TS reduction results. This result is 
due to the faster hydrolysis of corn stover at higher pH values. Wang 
et al. (2016) found that neutral pH was more favorable for sCOD accu­
mulation. Comparing TS and sCOD accumulation during pretreatment, 
at pH 5 and pH 6, corn stover was hydrolyzed every day during the 5 
d pretreatment, but the sCOD concentration in the hydrolysate rose and 
fell. This means that the speed of sCOD consumption was faster than 
sCOD generation, which negatively impacts methane production. Even 
at pH 7 and pH 8, the velocity and magnitude of sCOD increase were 
lower than TS reduction, indicating that sCOD was massively produced 
and consumed simultaneously. Considering these results, for maximum 
methane production, the pretreatment time should be no more than 2 d. 
VFAs are the most important products of hydrolysis and acidogenesis 
of corn stover during MMP. As the precursor of anaerobic methanation, 
VFA concentration and composition have a great impact on AD (Li et al., 
2020a). To be specific, total VFAs are calculated by adding the propi­
onic, acetic, isobutyric, butyric, isovaleric and valeric acid contents. 
Fig. 1c displays the mechanism of pH in VFAs composition and gener­
ation in corn stover pretreatment. The VFA accumulation trends are 
similar to those of the sCOD concentration of hydrolysate. A higher pH 
was beneficial to VFA accumulation. After 5 d of pretreatment, the 
concentrations of VFAs were 6.18, 9.09, 10.58, 13.22, and 10.44 g/L at 
pH 5, pH 6, pH 7, pH 8, and pH-U, respectively. Such findings were 
consistent with those obtained by Karthikeyan et al. (2016), where the 
VFA content within the traditional continuous stirred tank reactor 
increased by 35% at pH = 9 relative to that at pH = 6 in the processes of 
kitchen waste hydrolysis and acidification. 
The VFA:sCOD ratio is an indicator of acidogenesis. It was observed 
that the VFA:sCOD ratio in the hydrolysate gradually increased with the 
length of pretreatment. Initially, the proportion of VFAs equivalent to 
sCOD in total sCOD was 61.2%, but after 5 d of pretreatment, the pro­
portion increased to 87.6%, 96.2%, 87.5%, 90.4%, and 96.3% at pH 5, 
pH 6, pH 7, pH 8, and pH-U, respectively. This means acidogenesis was 
faster than hydrolysis, and that hydrolysis was the rate-limiting process. 
In addition, on the first day, the sCOD of the pH 5 pretreatment was the 
highest, whereas the amount of VFAs was the lowest, which means that 
lower pH had an inhibitory effect on acidogenic fermentation. 
In a previous study, pH was found to greatly influence the type of 
acidogenic fermentation (Li et al., 2020b). The present work indicated 
that pH significantly affected the VFA composition (Table 2). In all 
pretreatment samples, acetic acid had the largest proportion, accounting 
for 77%–86% of VFAs, followed by propionic acid. This result was 
similar to that of Wang et al. (2016), who found that the level of acetic 
and butyric acid, which accounted for 76.75% of total VFAs, was opti­
mized after the kitchen waste hydrolysis and acidification processes. The 
high acetic acid content is beneficial to AD as acetic acid, a precursor for 
methane production, contributes to 65%–95% of methane production 
(Weber et al., 1984). The proportion of propionic acid was most affected 
by pH control. A low pH value predicts the low propionic acid per­
centage, which may be due to a metabolic pathway shift at different pH 
values (Sawatdeenarunat et al., 2015). It was reported that propionic 
acid accumulation can inhibit methanogenesis, and that the promoted 
formation of acetate and the reduced accumulation of propionate were 
good for methane generation (Wang et al., 2006). The acetic acid:pro­
pionic acid ratio in the hydrolysate is regarded as an indicator of the 
stability of AD; a ratio above 2.0 is considered safe for AD (Wagner et al., 
2014). In this study, the propionic acid concentration and the acetic 
acid:propionic acid ratio were far from inhibitory levels, and this was to 
the advantage of the later utilization of VFA during methanogenesis. 
3.2.3. CMCase activity during pretreatment 
Extracellular cellulase activities were examined during MMP 
(Fig. 1e). The results showed that the inoculum had high CMCase ac­
tivity, and that all the test samples maintained high CMCase activity 
during pretreatment. The extracellular CMCase activities of pH 6 and pH 
5 hydrolysate were higher than those of the other pH values, but the 
higher extracellular CMCase activities did not lead to higher TS reduc­
tion, which means that extracellular CMCase activities cannot represent 
the actual cellulose hydrolysis ability in the MMP process. This is 
because, unlike cellulose-producing fungi, few bacteria can excrete 
extracellular cellulase. Most cellulases produced by bacteria are intra­
cellular enzymes, which are combined with the cytomembrane (Sadhu & 
Maiti, 2013). 
3.2.4. The effect of pH control on the microbial community structure during 
pretreatment 
Upon the completion of MMP at diverse pH values, we obtained the 
hydrolysate to analyze the structures of microbial communities. We 
assigned fragments of 16S rRNA gene at diverse taxa levels, ranging 
from phylum to genus. The microbial community structure of bacteria at 
different pH values at the phylum, class, order, and genus levels are 
illustrated in Fig. 2. MMP at different pH values greatly influenced 
bacterial community structure. Some strictly anaerobic and uncultured 
microbes vanished during pretreatment, accompanied by the prolifera­
tion of aerobic and facultative microbes. 
At the phylum level, Firmicutes, Bacteroidota, and Proteobacteria were 
dominant during pretreatment, accounting for 86%–99% of the bacte­
rial population. These bacteria are mainly facultative anaerobic bacte­
ria, which are widely active in various anaerobic and microaerobic 
degradation processes, and play a role in macromolecular hydrolysis and 
organic acid production (Ziganshin et al., 2013). In the initial mixed raw 
materials, the Firmicutes relative abundance was determined to be 70%. 
Firmicutes have been well-recognized to generate extracellular enzymes 
(such as protease, cellulase and lipase), and they play important roles in

lipid, lignin, protein and cellulose metabolism (Lim et al., 2014). This 
explains the high extracellular cellulase activity in the initial hydroly­
sate. After 5 d of MMP, the dominant bacteria in hydrolysate shifted 
from Firmicutes to Bacteroidota at pH 6, pH 7, pH 8, and pH-U. The 
relative abundance of Firmicutes reduced to 10%–15% and that of Bac­
teroidota increased to 71%–76%. A metaproteomic study found that 
Bacteroidota is a common bacteria phylum in the decomposition of 
lignocellulose raw materials, which participates in hydrolyzing poly­
saccharides such as cellulose and hemicellulose, and suitable for a 
neutral pH environment (Hanreich et al., 2013). This explains our 
findings, at pH 6, pH 7, pH 8, and pH-U, Bacteroidota was more suitable 
for the microaeration pretreatment conditions in this study, and had 
good hydrolysis ability for lignocellulose. In contrast, at the pH 5 con­
ditions, the Firmicutes relative abundance was kept at an increased level 
relative to those under additional pretreatments, which is due to Fir­
micutes having stronger resistance to low pH than other microbial 
communities (Pervin et al., 2013). 
At the class and order levels, the microbial community structure of 
bacteria of all pH-controlled MMPs also greatly changed. After 5 d of 
MMP at pH 6, pH 7, pH 8, and pH-U, strictly anaerobic Clostridia and 
Lactobacillus were reduced, and the abundance of Bacteroidia increased. 
At pH 5, Firmicutes-Bacilli proliferated due to strong resistance. 
At the genus level, unidentified microbial communities accounted 
for the majority of the bacterial population in the initial mixed raw 
materials. After 5 d of pretreatment, Proteiniphilum, Rummeliibacillus, 
and Prevotella were the dominant microbial communities. At pH 6, pH 7, 
pH 8, and pH-U MMP, Proteiniphilum increased rapidly, accounting for 
46%–54.0% of the bacterial population. Proteiniphilum represents a vital 
genus of the Bacteroidota phylum, and it can promote hemicellulose 
decomposition and use the N-containing substrates for generating acetic 
acid and NH3 (He et al., 2017). At pH 5, Rummeliibacillus and Prevotella 
proliferated rapidly, accounting for 46.0 and 33.3% of the bacterial 
population after 5 d of pretreatment. Rummeliibacillus can secrete mul­
tiple cellulase and hemicellulase enzymes, which are widely used in the 
acidification of lignocellulosic material (Weimer et al., 2011). Many 
articles suggest that Prevotella are important acidogenic bacteria, and 
that low pH is beneficial for Prevotella (Lebuhn et al., 2014; Won et al., 
2013). 
Some studies suggest that increased hydrolysis could possibly be 
associated with fungi existing within the inoculum, and they can 
decompose organic biomass in the microaerobic environment (Peces 
et al., 2016). Fungi can decompose polysaccharides such as cellulose and 
hemicellulose through producing the extracellular enzymes. In the 
microaerobic conditions, fungi possibly possess the partial depolymer­
ization complex structures in simple organic molecules; as a result, more 
corn stover is available for fermentative bacteria. Fig. 3 shows the fungal 
community structure at different pH levels at phylum and genus scales. 
At the phylum level, Ascomycota (43.4%) was the most abundant, fol­
lowed by Basidiomycota. Ascomycota are the most abundant composting 
phyla in cow manure, food and garden waste, and sewage sludge (Meng 
et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018), which produce various enzymes to 
degrade hemicellulose and cellulose and effectively use the substrate 
nutrients (Singh et al., 2003). Basidiomycota represent the vital 
contributing factors to the functions of the ecosystem at several levels, 
which stand for the main lignin degraders (Xing et al., 2020). Initially, at 
pH 6, pH 7 and pH 8 MMP, Ascomycota were represented by the Tri­
choderma genus, which represented the omnipresent cellulosic sub­
stance colonizers that are usually detected in the presence of decayed 
plant materials (Kubicek et al., 2008). Under pH-U and pH 5 conditions, 
the microbial community structure of fungi at the genus level changed 
significantly, indicating that pH change greatly impacts fungal com­
munity structure. 
Ammonia concentration is also an important factor in changing mi­
crobial diversity and activity. To evaluate the effect of NH4-N on MMP, 
the ammonia concentration under different pH control strategies was 
measured. As shown in Fig. 1d, the ammonia concentration remained 
low and should not have an important impact on the MMP process. 
In summary, at different pH pretreatment conditions, different mi­
crobial community structures were formed, causing changes in the hy­
drolysis capacity and pathways and leading to different soluble 
compositions and VFA patterns (Calicioglu et al., 2018).

3.3. Effect of pH and pretreatment time on methane yield 
The methane production during 20 d of mesophilic AD of corn stover 
under different pH pretreatments for different lengths of time (0, 6, 12, 
24, and 48 h) is shown in Fig. 4. The experimental data fitted with Eq. 
(1) are shown in Table 3. 
The methane yield potential was significantly related to pretreat­
ment time and not significantly (p greater than 0.05) related to pH. After 
6 h pretreatment, all methane yields during 20 d AD (B20) of pretreated 
corn stover were higher than that of the no-pretreatment control except 
for the pH 5 sample; the methane yield sequence of the samples was pH- 
U > pH 6 > pH 7 > pH 8 > pH 5. The highest cumulative methane yield 
arrived at 146.5 mL/g TS for the pH-U pretreatment, which was 10.2% 
higher than that of the control. Nevertheless, the methane yield poten­
tial resulting from linear regression had different features. The methane 
yield potentials of pH-U, pH 5, and pH 6 were essentially equal to the 
control, whereas the k of pH-U, pH 6, pH 7, and pH 8 were all higher 
than those of the control, which represented a higher hydrolysis rate of 
AD through MMP. 
After 12 h pretreatment, all pH treatments had greater B20 of pre­
treated corn stover than the 6 h pretreatment counterparts except for pH 
5. Both the methane yield potential and hydrolysis rate were enhanced

pretreatment, which was 25.0% higher than that of the control. For the 
pH-U pretreatment, the highest methane yield potential was 174.3 mL/g 
TS, which was 16.6% higher than that of the control. The enhancement 
was consistent with the results of Fu et al. (2016), who found that the 
maximum cumulative methane yield was 16.5% higher than that of the 
control using a microaeration strategy for the AD of corn stover. 
After 24 h pretreatment, even when the initial methane production 
was higher than the control, both the B20 and methane yield potential of 
pretreated corn stover were lower or slightly higher than that of the 
control. This means that the overconsumption during the pretreatment 
process negatively affects methane production. The lowest B20 was 
122.0 mL/g TS for the pH 8 pretreatment, which was 8.2% lower than 
that of the control. 
The methane production results of the 48-h pretreatment verified the 
speculation detailed in Section 3.2.2, as the negative effect on methane 
yield potential by over respiration dominated the pretreatment effect. 
Even when the sCOD was higher than the control and the 24 h pre­
treatments, the final methane production was lower than the control due 
to overconsumption during the pretreatment process. The greatest 
negative effect (12.7%) was detected at 109.2 mL/g TS for the pH 8 
pretreatment, which was 17.8% lower than that of the control. 
Overall, at pH 5, MMP changed the methane production rate, but not 
the methane yield potential. Among pH 6, pH 7, pH 8, and pH-U pre­
treatment, pH had an effect on AD, but the effect was not significant (p 
greater than 0.05). Pretreatment time significantly affected (p < 0.05) 
methane yield potential, and 12 h pretreatment was the optimal pre­
treatment time, improving both methane yield potential and methane 
production rate. Hence, the methane yield results of the optimization 
study imply that MMP is a simple and cost-effective approach for the 
effective improvement of anaerobic biological degradability for recal­
citrant lignocellulosic biomass. pH and pretreatment time led to both 
positive and negative AD results. The threshold level of microaeration 
pretreatment may differ across diverse AD systems, which must be 
determined for preventing over-pretreatment. 
4. Conclusions 
MMP resulted in the metabolism of complex lignocellulose substrates 
by facilitating the proliferation of bacteria and fungi with hydrolysis and 
acidogenic abilities, which led to a higher AD rate. The proliferation of 
acidogenic and VFA-utilizing bacteria and aerobic respiration increased 
substrate reduction, which make against to improving methane yield 
potential. pH altered hydrolysis and metabolic pathways by affecting 
microbial diversity. Both pH and pretreatment time affected hydrolysis 
and methane yield. Maximum methane yield potential was found at 12 h 
pretreatment with a pH of 8, and was 174.3 mL/g TS and 16.6% higher 
than that of the control.
